title: He refused a judgeship
hookLine: reports say Abu Hanifa refused to be a judge for the caliph and was imprisoned

lines: HE SAYS NO, AND NO AGAIN.
cards: The offer comes with power: a judgeship, with the caliph's backing, over property, marriages and punishments. The man being offered it is a cloth merchant and a teacher with students of his own in Kufa. He says no.
He's asked again, and he says no again. The reports differ on the details, but they agree on the shape: the pressure grew, and so did the price of refusing. His school would go on to fill courts.
The founder himself would not sit in the judge's seat.

teach.b: His biographers tell of a governor of Iraq who wanted him as a judge and had him beaten when he refused, and of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur pressing him again and having him imprisoned.
Some reports say he died in that prison. The accounts don't all agree, and historians weigh them differently, so it's fair to say: this is what the reports say. Then a story people tell.
Abu Hanifa told the caliph he wasn't fit for the post. You're lying, said the caliph.

teach.h: YOU'VE JUST RULED THAT I'M UNFIT.
teach.b: Then you've just ruled that I'm unfit, he answered, because a liar can't be a judge. Whether or not it happened in those words, it shows how he's remembered: quick, calm, impossible to corner. Why refuse at all?
A hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud says whoever is made a judge among people has been slaughtered without a knife.
Scholars read it as a warning that judging endangers the soul: a wrong ruling could take someone's home or someone's life. Some pious scholars ran from the post for that reason.
Others, like Abu Yusuf, accepted it and tried to judge justly, and the tradition honors them too. Readers see one more reason: a judge appointed by a ruler can be pushed by that ruler.
Refusing kept Abu Hanifa's judgment his own, while the school he built went on to staff courts across empires.

how: Muslim biographers tell of Abu Hanifa refusing the judgeship under pressure, and of other scholars who avoided the post out of fear of judging wrongly, while honoring those who took it and judged justly.

games.q: what does “he refused a judgeship” mean?
o: Abu Hanifa turned down the post of judge, despite pressure
Abu Yusuf turned down a caliph's offer to lead the courts
Abu Hanifa was removed as judge for ruling against a caliph

games.q: he refused a judgeship — tap the pairs.
p: a liar can't be a judge
his answer, in a story people tell
a hadith about being made a judge

s: every account of Abu Hanifa's refusal agrees on the details
the reports differ; they agree on the shape: refusal, pressure, punishment.
a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud warns that whoever is made a judge is slaughtered without a knife
judging was seen as a danger to the soul.
the tradition condemns every scholar who became a judge
it honors those who took the post and judged justly, like Abu Yusuf.

games.q: you're Abu Hanifa. the caliph says you're lying when you call yourself unfit to judge. what do you answer?
o: then you've ruled that I'm unfit, since a liar can't be a judge.
games.why: in the story people tell, he turns the accusation into his own proof. whether or not it happened in those words, it's how he's remembered.

practice: Think of a role someone wants you to take that doesn't fit: covering for a friend, taking sides in a family fight, a yes that would cost something you won't trade.

Find the sentence you'd use to say no, short and kind, and say it once in your head, noticing your shoulders as you do; if the role turns out to be right after all, notice that too. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: He refused a judgeship. Reports say Abu Hanifa turned down the post of judge, under pressure from a governor and a caliph, and was beaten and imprisoned for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a judge, the one who decides a case; the post Abu Hanifa refused.

carryVoice: Your line: he refused the post. Keeping your judgment your own can carry a price. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 3571–3572 (whoever is made a judge has been slaughtered without a knife)
Biographical reports on Abu Hanifa (e.g. al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, Tarikh Baghdad)
